# PL/SQL

Oracle's procedural extension to SQL: block-structured, statically typed against the schema, and
executed inside the database rather than in a client. Used throughout `sql/03_plsql/` and
`sql/04_object_relational/` in [[oracle-database-laboratories]], and nowhere else in this source set.

## The unit of everything is a block

```
DECLARE  … declarations, including local procedures and functions
BEGIN    … statements
EXCEPTION … handlers
END; /
```

Anonymous blocks run as-is from [[sql-plus]]; named blocks become procedures, functions, packages and
triggers. Blocks nest, and nesting is the idiomatic way to scope an exception: the chief-walking
exercise wraps its inner lookup in its own `BEGIN … EXCEPTION` so that walking off the top of the
hierarchy ends the chain rather than propagating `NO_DATA_FOUND` out of the loop.

The trailing `/` is not decoration. Inside a type or package body a bare semicolon ends the enclosed
statement, not the body, so a file without the slashes cannot be run as a script at all.

## The features the repo leans on

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| `%TYPE`, `%ROWTYPE` | anchor variables to the schema, so a column widening does not need an edit |
| Cursors | explicit and `FOR`-loop forms — see [[plsql-cursors]] |
| Exceptions | predefined, user-defined, `SQLCODE`/`SQLERRM`, `RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR` — see [[plsql-exception-handling]] |
| Collections | `TABLE OF … INDEX BY VARCHAR2` associative arrays; nested tables for name lists |
| Packages | spec plus body; package variables persist for the session, which is both the feature and the hazard |
| Triggers | row, statement, compound, autonomous — see [[database-triggers]] |
| `EXECUTE IMMEDIATE` | dynamic DDL, used in the teardown scripts |
| Object types | `MEMBER FUNCTION` / `MEMBER PROCEDURE`, `SELF IN OUT` — see [[object-relational-model]] |

## Name resolution is the language's sharpest edge

Where a PL/SQL identifier and a column share a name, **the PL/SQL identifier wins**. That turns
`WHERE name = name_band` into a tautology: the duplicate check passes on everything, silently, with no
error anywhere. The repo's two defences are both worth copying — qualify every predicate with its
table name, and deliberately name `INTO` targets apart from the columns they read (`allowed_min`
versus `min_mice`).

This is the PL/SQL-specific instance of a general failure mode: a check that runs, reports success and
checks nothing. See [[tests-that-pass-for-the-wrong-reason]].

## Practical notes from the source

- **Reading an associative array at an unassigned key raises `NO_DATA_FOUND`** rather than returning
  `NULL`. Every read needs an `EXISTS` guard; `NVL` does not help.
- **`SHOW ERRORS PACKAGE BODY <name>`** after a create is how you see why a body compiled invalid —
  the `CREATE` itself reports only "created with compilation errors".
- **Package state persists across statements in a session**, which is exactly what the three-trigger
  design exploits and exactly why it is fragile. A compound trigger's declaration section
  reinitialises per statement instead — see [[compound-trigger-over-package-state]].
- **A `MEMBER PROCEDURE` receives `SELF` as `IN OUT` by default**, so an attribute assignment mutates
  the caller's instance.

## Where it sits against the alternatives

PL/SQL puts logic next to the data: no round trip, no ORM, transactional by default. The cost is
portability (none of this survives an engine change), testability (there is no test framework here —
correctness is asserted in comments and by running the scripts), and reviewability (logic in a trigger
executes without appearing at any call site). The repo's own comments repeatedly weigh those trades
in place — [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].
